members.tone: Praises taste without naming what it consists of - which is how it also flatters the speaker's own.
Sets a bar and implies others fall below it; the compliment has a history.
The British spelling; the same compliment with the same history.
Praises the work, not the birth - it says the taste was acquired on purpose.
Warmer and less effortful than cultivated; it suggests taste that was absorbed rather than studied.
Faintly pitying since the nineteenth century - shabby-genteel is never far away.
The plain positive of the group: it describes conduct anyone can manage, and asks for no admiration.
A back-formation from uncouth, and almost always a joke; nobody is seriously called couth.
Mocks refinement as performance - the word describes the walk, and means the person.
The most contemptuous word here; the invented sound does the sneering.
Disapproves gently: correct manners held so tightly they have become a fault.
British and withering - sweetness pushed past charm into embarrassment.
Reports the feeling without judging it; the mildest and least loaded word in the family.
Points at whoever caused it - the anger is presented as a reasonable response.
Puts the blame on the other party outright: someone did this to them.
Formal and slightly distant, as though reported rather than witnessed.
The anger has taken the person over; it describes a state, not an opinion.
The everyday word for full anger - vivid, and still sympathetic to whoever feels it.
Like enraged, but it keeps the cause in view: something did this to them.
Borrows the language of madness; the anger is presented as beyond reason.
Of a mood rather than an outburst - settled, silent and unpleasant to be near.
Judges the character, not the moment: a person built this way, from the old humours.
The formal word for a short fuse; it condemns a standing disposition.
Comic and deflating - it makes the anger look faintly ridiculous.
The plain, unqualified praise - it credits both the giving and the spirit behind it.
Praises the disposition rather than any particular gift; often said of institutions.
Rare and warm: the giving is presented as coming from feeling, not duty.
Praise with a shrug - big of you can be sincere or sarcastic, and often is.
Unfashionable and entirely sincere; it praises the person, not the sum.
Biblical in flavour, and hard to use now without irony.
Abundance more than kindness - the giving is a matter of plenty.
Describes the habit of giving easily, with no comment on why.
Of a sum or a gesture - it praises the scale, and implies it exceeded what was owed.
Modern and slightly therapeutic; it names a personality type.
Of portions and allowances, not politics - though the political sense now shadows every use.
A vivid old word: the hand is not closed, and neither is the person.
Mildly critical, and often affectionate - it can be said of a child or a stain.
Colder and more formal than stubborn; it withholds the affection stubborn allows.
The refusal is a refusal to be reformed, and the speaker has given up on it.
British and furious - it says the obstruction is the whole point.
Almost fond, in the way one is fond of a difficult relative; the word is too comic to wound.
From Bolshevik: it frames the refusal as insubordination rather than character.
British; it makes the defiance sound adolescent, which is the insult.
Adds stupidity to the charge - not just unmoving but unable to see why it should move.
The same accusation with a harder image; rare, and unkind about the head as well.
The most contemptuous of the stubborn words: obstinacy treated as stupidity.
The same refusal to yield, entirely admired - dogged is what stubborn is called when it wins.
Unyielding and unsmiling; it judges the manner as much as the will.
The plain accusation: attention was owed and not paid.
Often neutral or even approving elsewhere; here it means attention that was never offered.
Formal and cool - it reports the shallowness without raising its voice.
Barely a judgement: a passing glance is short, not necessarily careless.
The work was done to be seen to be done; it accuses the motive, not the skill.
Cuts twice - shallow work, and often a shallow person implied behind it.
Blames the absence of a method rather than the absence of effort.
The sound of the word carries the speed; brisk contempt rather than anger.
Old and severe: it implies a standard has been abandoned, not merely missed.
The everyday version, mild enough to say to someone's face.
Warnings existed and were ignored; it presumes there was something to heed.
The gravest here - it implies danger, and appears in law for that reason.
Describes the state, not the person - machinery and money are idle too.
British and total: the laziness is presented as going all the way through.
The same accusation in the plainer word; no part of the person is exempted.
A do-nothing word for a do-nothing; it condemns from a distance.
The softest of the real accusations - it sounds almost like a temperament.
The everyday charge, and a moral one: the work was there and was not done.
More often used of arguments than people, where it means pointless rather than idle.
Names one of the seven deadly sins; the laziness is a fault of the soul.
Political and accusing - it belongs to arguments about who deserves support.
Comic rather than damning; the failing is a lack of spirit, not of will.
The same idleness, admired - because it is assumed to have been paid for.
Purely factual: not currently occupied, with no view taken on why.
Praise for meeting the standard; it says nothing about warmth, and sometimes implies its absence.
Old-fashioned and slightly schoolroom - it praises training more than instinct.
Credits the upbringing; the compliment reaches past the person to whoever raised them.
Formal warmth, with a whiff of chivalry - it praises the manner as a kind of respect.
The warmest here - courtesy extended when it need not have been.
Weak from overuse; it now praises so mildly that it can read as faint disappointment.
The plain word, and the honest one: approval expressed and meant.
An old sense - to sing something in a full round voice; the modern internet sense is unrelated.
Borrows the gesture from the military; it praises formally and briefly, as an act of respect.
Public by nature - the praise is performed so that others see it given.
Church Latin behind it; it lifts the praise onto a ceremonial register.
Praise at length and without reservation - the enthusiasm is part of the meaning.
Raises the subject rather than merely approving of them; close to worship.
Turns critical the moment the object does not deserve it - glorifies violence is the usual company it keeps.
About the volume, not the sincerity: praise announced rather than felt.
Praise with a purpose: the compliment is a means to something.
Flattery with coaxing added - the praise is a lever being worked.
Ceremonial praise, expected by the occasion, which discounts it slightly.
The British spelling of the same funeral-shaped praise.
Small, direct and social - one remark, given to a person's face.
Casual and dismissive; it implies the criticism is cheap and possibly unfair.
The neutral verb - it names the act without saying whether it was deserved.
The British spelling of the same neutral verb.
Methodical rather than angry: the thing is taken to pieces on purpose.
Official and procedural - it happens on a record, from someone with the standing to do it.
Formal condemnation by a body; the weight comes from the institution.
Rare and legalistic; it frames the fault as very nearly a crime.
The metaphor is an animal attack - it says the criticism went past its target.
Headline language: loud, public and short, with no pretence of fairness.
Names an actual punishment - public humiliation, deliberately staged.
The most extreme word here, and it casts the target as a victim rather than a culprit.
Gentle and improving; the point is to correct, and the relationship survives it.
A mild, old-fashioned rebuke - correction rather than attack.
The rarer verb beside the common noun; the same quiet correction.
The standard accusation: the speaker is impressed with themselves and has said so.
Commercial - the boasting is on behalf of something being sold.
Nearly extinct outside swashbuckling; it suggests noise and swagger rather than claims.
Implies the boast is invented as well as unwelcome.
Blunter and more childish than boast; the word itself is faintly playground.
The boasting is empty and long-winded - the complaint is about the volume.
Chiefly American; blowing one's own horn, with the same air of hot air.
Loud claims covering weakness; it implies the speaker will not back them up.
Elevated and old; the boasting is grand enough to sound almost heroic.
From Gascony, whose people were reputed braggarts - a learned word for a common fault.
Inflation rather than pride: the thing is made to seem larger than it is.
The cruellest here - the pleasure depends on someone else having lost.
Nearly neutral, and the only word that lets the winning be the point rather than the gloating.
The image is a farmyard bird at dawn: loud, repetitive and pleased with itself.
The neutral verb; everything else in the family adds a judgement to it.
Rude by default in English - the length of the look is what makes it an offence.
Casual and brief, with no attitude attached.
The British phrasing of the same brief, unloaded glance.
An invitation to look at something ridiculous; the judgement is on the thing, not the looking.
Directional and plain, though the phrase carries a second, wistful life.
The literal version, used where the wistful sense would confuse.
Neutral in form, but the turning away is itself the act.
Surveying rather than fixing on anything; no judgement either way.
Long and absorbed - the word grants the looker something worth looking at.
Formal and considering; the eyes are doing the work of the mind.
The looking has become thinking - attention paid rather than merely directed.
Sustained and purposeful, and neutral until context makes it protective or sinister.
Condemns the looker outright: the look is sexual, unwanted and obvious.
The neutral verb - it records the act and leaves the merits open.
Implies the objection is loud and probably futile.
An old sense surviving mainly in plaintive and plaintiff; to complain formally.
The complaint is unasked-for and delivered at length.
The older English spelling of kvetch, now rare.
From Yiddish, and affectionate as often as not - the complaining is a known habit.
Repetition is the offence: the complaint is not wrong, only relentless.
Small, repeated and birdlike; it makes the complaint sound trivial by design.
Openly sexist: it casts a wife as the tormentor and a husband as her victim.
The complaint is made behind the person's back, which is the whole accusation.
Coarse and common; it dismisses the complaint by the word used to name it.
Attacks the sound and the character together - it says the complaint is beneath answering.
British, and it makes the complaining sound wet and wearing.
The complaint as noise: continuous, and no longer being listened to.
